transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-30 15:00 PT | Duration: ~57m | Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Jules Park (Redwood CSM); Dr. Priya Nair (CISO), Evan Cole (Dir Eng), Maya Ruiz (DevOps), Samir Patel (Security Architect)

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: okay everyone thanks for carving out time, uh this is Lena from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. we wanna run through the pen test outcomes, align on the vuln triage and then walk through our KMS/ encryption roadmap. quick sound check?

[00:10] Dr. Priya Nair: sounds good, priya here, can hear you.

[00:15] Evan Cole: evan, good to go.

[00:20] Marcus Chen: hey all, marcus from the SE team, i'll own the technical bits.

[00:25] Lena Ortiz: great. quick agenda: 1) summary of pen test findings and remediation status, 2) patch cadence and SDLC controls, 3) KMS/encryption design and audit logs, 4) next steps. we'll try to keep to 45-60 min.

[00:40] Lena Ortiz: to start, we cut the summary doc and i'll drop the link after — high level: two high severity findings were raised but both were remediated in the latest patch: outdated TLS cipher config on the control plane, and an insecure dependency in our telemetry ingest. those have fixes in prod last week.

[01:05] Samir Patel: can you repeat the telemetry detail? was that an OSS library?

[01:12] Marcus Chen: yeah, that was an open-source collector that had a path traversal vuln. we patched the dependency to the patched minor version and added a scanner rule. note that the exploit required a mis-configured ingest endpoint, which we closed.

[01:28] Dr. Priya Nair: ok good, what's the verification process? do you have re-test evidence?

[01:35] Marcus Chen: we ran an internal verification pass and our external pentest vendor re-validated the two fixes last Friday. i'll attach the re-test notes in the follow-up. it's in the remediation tracker we shared.

[01:48] Evan Cole: how are you tracking remaining medium/low items? we want to see triage, owners, and timelines.

[01:54] Jules Park: we pushed a spreadsheet and a jira export. for Quantum Medics specifically we can push a CSV into your tracker — but we'll need one of your folks to create an epic for the pen-test work so we can link remediation tickets.

[02:10] Maya Ruiz: yeah, i'll own that, maya here. we'll spin the epic and assign to our squads. timeline-wise we typically do two-week sprints, do you recommend any hotfix window?

[02:22] Marcus Chen: for medium severity we recommend patch within 30 days and for high severity 7 days, with a canary deploy step. Redwood supports canary by route/model in the console so you can limit blast radius.

[02:38] Samir Patel: when you say canary by route/model, is that per inference model or per service? need to be precise cause we have regulatory workflows.

[02:47] Marcus Chen: good call — i mean per deployed model variant and route. so you can route 10% of traffic to the new build, validate logs and metrics, then bump to 100%. for regulated flows you can pin to dedicated capacity as well.

[03:05] Dr. Priya Nair: let's talk KMS. our security team requires customer-managed keys (BYOK) with HSM-backed rotation and audit trail. can Redwood integrate with our cloud KMS?

[03:16] Lena Ortiz: short answer yes — Redwood Private supports KMS integrations and we have documented HSM flows. Marcus, do you wanna walk briefly through the design?

[03:23] Marcus Chen: sure. at a high level we support tinctures — sorry i mean the standard envelope encryption: model artifacts and logs are encrypted at rest with a data key that is itself encrypted by your KMS key. we support AWS KMS, Google KMS, and on-prem HSMs that expose PKCS#11. We also have an optional mTLS channel for key fetches and audit logging on the key access.

[03:50] Dr. Priya Nair: you said audit logging — is key usage logged in a way that can be exported to our SIEM? we need immutable logs, retention 7 years for certain datasets.

[04:02] Marcus Chen: yes, KMS access events are surfaced in our audit logs; we can forward logs to your SIEM (splunk, sumo, or a syslog endpoint). retention defaults to 90 days in the hosted offering but in Private we can configure longer retention and ship to your log store so you control retention.

[04:22] Samir Patel: any concerns with latency when calling customer KMS for every decryption? our inference paths are latency sensitive.

[04:30] Marcus Chen: we do not call the KMS on every inference. Redwood uses envelope encryption and caches decrypted data keys in memory in the node's secure enclave for a configurable window (KV cache). we also rotate the cached keys at a policy you set. so KMS calls are amortized.

[04:48] Evan Cole: what's the caching TTL and how do you balance it with rotation requirements? we need to meet a 24-hour rotation policy.

[04:56] Marcus Chen: TTLs are configurable — common pattern is 1-6 hours cache TTL, with automatic rekeying at 24 hours to meet rotation. we can surface a policy that rotates data keys daily while still keeping low per-inference overhead.

[05:14] Maya Ruiz: is the KV cache encrypted in-memory? if someone dumps process memory is the key at risk?

[05:21] Marcus Chen: good question — we keep keys in an OS protected memory region and use platform cryptography (e.g., Linux mlock, and optionally a TEE where available). in Private deployments you can enable enclave mode for extra protection. i'll add the exact mem-protection details to the runbook.

[05:43] Dr. Priya Nair: what about RBAC and SSO? we need SCIM provisioning, SAML SSO, and admin RBAC with separation of duties.

[05:52] Jules Park: Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. our RBAC model has tenancy-level roles, project roles, and token scopes. tokens can be scoped to read-only or inference-only.

[06:06] Samir Patel: can we enforce IP allowlists and org-level MFA?

[06:12] Lena Ortiz: yes — IP allowlists are supported at the org and project level for Private and Dedicated. MFA for user logins is enforced via your IdP; we also have a built-in 2FA option for hosted accounts.

[06:24] Evan Cole: audit logs — how granular are they? we need to show token usage, model version changes, and admin role changes.

[06:32] Marcus Chen: audit logs include user actions, token issuance and usage, model rollouts, config changes, and KMS key access events. we give token-level breakdowns for cost and latency; we can also export raw logs to your SIEM.

[06:46] Dr. Priya Nair: good. on data residency: we're planning EU-only PHI processing. can you guarantee that data and logs for a given project never leave eu-west-1?

[06:57] Marcus Chen: in Private and Dedicated we can pin region. hosted API has region selection for residency, but for strict EU-only we recommend Private deployment in your VPC or our EU region under a dedicated tenancy. we'll include contractual language in the DPA.

[07:12] Maya Ruiz: any recommendations for secure SDLC? the pen-test vendor flagged some infra-as-code drift that made a staging cluster exposed.

[07:20] Lena Ortiz: common patterns: gated merges, terraform plan in CI with policy-as-code (opa/conftest), automated drift detection, and immutable infra rebuilds. Redwood's infra repo uses automated policies and we can share our baseline templates.

[07:34] Samir Patel: the vendor also called out container runtime privileges — privilege escalation via mis-set capabilities. what's Redwood's hardening baseline?

[07:42] Marcus Chen: containers run as non-root by default, and we apply seccomp and seccli (sorry seccomp and read-only file systems). we also use image signing and a denylist for known bad packages. for Private we can show SBOMs on demand.

[08:00] Evan Cole: about SBOM — can you produce SBOMs per release and map them to CVEs?

[08:07] Marcus Chen: yes we generate SBOMs (cycloneDX format) and map to CVEs in our vulnerability tracker. the pen-test items already have CVE references where applicable.

[08:20] Dr. Priya Nair: on the remaining medium items, we need evidence of remediation and regression tests. what's your recommended evidence package?

[08:28] Lena Ortiz: typical package: fix description, patched branch/PR links, CI green build, re-test notes from vendor, and if applicable, updated config snippets or runbook entries. we'll assemble that per item.

[08:42] Maya Ruiz: ok, for compliance we also need to see your SOC 2 Type II — specifically the monitoring and change control docs.

[08:50] Lena Ortiz: understood, i'll push the full SOC 2 bundle plus a short 2-page summary of change control evidence.

[08:58] Samir Patel: regarding patch cadence, we run monthly platform upgrades but hotfixes for security — what's Redwood's recommended cadence if we want minimum user disruption?

[09:07] Marcus Chen: recommended cadence: monthly non-security upgrades in a maintenance window; security hotfixes applied immediately with a canary phase (7-14 day rollback window depending on risk). for infra-as-a-service we can coordinate maintenance with you.

[09:22] Evan Cole: do you do upstream patch testing against our workloads? like run our smoke tests after a patch?

[09:28] Marcus Chen: we offer a partner testing hook: you can upload a lightweight smoke test harness that runs in the canary. for Dedicated/Private customers we can run your smoke tests in the canary stage as part of the rollout.

[09:42] Dr. Priya Nair: sounds good. one more item — encryption in-transit. vendor said TLS 1.2 with modern ciphers only. do you support TLS 1.3?

[09:50] Marcus Chen: yes TLS 1.3 by default, and we disable weak ciphers. the earlier finding was an older control plane endpoint which was inadvertently left on TLS 1.2 — that's been fixed.

[10:02] Lena Ortiz: i'm going to read back a short summary and proposed next steps. first, high severity items remediated and re-tested; medium/low items documented and a Jira epic to be created by Quantum Medics; KMS integration supported with envelope encryption and key caching, audit logs exportable to your SIEM; RBAC/SSO/SCIM supported; region pinning recommended for EU PHI; patch cadence: monthly plus hotfixes with canary and optional smoke test hook.

[10:29] Dr. Priya Nair: that captures it, thanks. couple clarifications — we want the runbook for KMS mem protection and the exact log schema for key events.

[10:39] Marcus Chen: i'll include both — runbook and a sample audit log schema (fields: timestamp, actor, action, resource, result, request_id, key_id).

[10:50] Lena Ortiz: next steps recap: Lena will send SOC2 and remediation summary (due 2026-07-02); Marcus prepares KMS diagram and runbook (due 2026-07-09); Maya will create Jira epic (due 2026-07-07); schedule a follow-up 2hr KMS deep dive the week of 2026-07-13.

[11:10] Evan Cole: one ask — can you include a short appendix about performance impact of KMS integration, like p99 latency delta with different cache TTLs?

[11:17] Marcus Chen: yes i'll add sample benchmarks: p50/p95/p99 for 0s, 1h, 6h cache TTL and estimated additional requests to KMS.

[11:28] Maya Ruiz: thanks, that's helpful.

[11:31] Lena Ortiz: any final questions?

[11:33] Samir Patel: none from me. thanks for the recap.

[11:36] Dr. Priya Nair: all good, thank you.

[11:40] Lena Ortiz: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule. meeting adjourned.

Transcript notes: occasional transcription artifacts ("tinctures" for "structures", "KV cash" for "KV cache") present; speaker attribution approximated in places.
